title: The Bliss at the End of Union with Shakti
sanskrit:
शविसंगमसंऺुब्धशक्त्यािेशािसावनकम् ।
यत्सुखम् ब्रह्मतत्त्वस्य तत्सुखम् स्वाक्यमुच्यते ॥ ६९ ॥
translation: The bliss that comes at the conclusion of the influx of power, when energy is stirred by union with Śakti—that bliss, they say, is the very bliss of the Brahman-principle.
intent_summary: Recognize the culminating bliss of awakened energy and union as identical with the bliss of ultimate reality.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that a peak moment of deep energetic or intimate union can reveal something sacred. Rather than seeing such bliss as merely physical or emotional, it invites you to recognize it as sharing the nature of the highest reality. The practice is to notice the depth of the experience without shrinking it into a private event.
scholar_explanation: Śakti-saṅgama here may imply ritual, yogic, or subtle inner union; the emphasis falls on the avasānika, the terminal or culminating phase of śaktyāveśa, possession or infusion by power. The resulting sukha is identified with brahma-tattva-sukha, a hallmark Kaula assertion that the highest nondual realization can be accessed through intensified śākta experience. This is not hedonism but the sacralization of climax as a moment of ego-dissolution and recognition.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Remembered Erotic Bliss as Flood of Ananda
sanskrit:
ऱेहनामन्थनाकोटै् स्त्रीसुखस्य भरात्स्मृते् ।
शक्त्यभािेऽवऩ देिेवश भिेदानन्दसम्प्लि् ॥ ७० ॥
translation: Through kissing, rubbing, and other acts, when the fullness of woman's pleasure is remembered, then even in the absence of Śakti, O Goddess, there may arise a flood of bliss.
intent_summary: Use even the vivid memory of intense erotic bliss as a support for awakening into overwhelming spiritual joy.
beginner_explanation: The verse says that even remembering a powerful moment of pleasure can awaken a strong inner current of bliss. It is not insisting on outer action; memory itself can become the doorway. The key is to stay with the energy of the experience and let it expand beyond personal desire.
scholar_explanation: Lehana, manthana, and related erotic acts are invoked not as ends in themselves but as sources of a recollected plenitude of śṛṅgāra-sukha. Even in the absence of the actual śakti-partner, smṛti can reactivate ānanda-samplava, a flood of bliss suitable for contemplative transmutation. This reflects the Kaula strategy of interiorizing ritual-erotic experience into autonomous yogic realization.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Dissolving into Arisen Joy
sanskrit:
आनन्दे महवत प्राप्ते दृष्टे िा िान्धिे वचरात् ।
आनन्दमुद्गतम् ध्यात्वा तल्लयस्तन्मना भिेत् ॥ ७१ ॥
translation: When great joy is attained, or when a dear relative or beloved one is seen after a long time, meditating on the joy that has arisen, one should dissolve into that; thus one's mind becomes of that nature.
intent_summary: Use a naturally arising surge of joy as the doorway for meditative absorption until the mind merges into that bliss.
beginner_explanation: Sometimes happiness appears suddenly and strongly, like when you meet someone you deeply love after a long separation. Instead of just enjoying the event, this verse says to notice the feeling of joy itself and rest in it. If you stay with the feeling without chasing thoughts, your mind can sink into a deeper peace behind the emotion.
scholar_explanation: This dhāraṇā takes mahānanda arising from worldly reunion as an upāya. The instruction is not attachment to the object but contemplation of the उद्गत आनन्द itself, allowing laya of mind into the rasa of consciousness. It reflects the Trika principle that intense affect, when freed from vikalpa and object-fixation, can reveal Bhairava as one's own ānanda-svarūpa.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Expansion Through Sensory Delight
sanskrit:
जववधऩानकृतोल्लासरसानन्दविजृम्भणात् ।
भाियेद्भवरतािस्थां महानन्दस्ततो भिेत् ॥ ७२ ॥
translation: From the expansion of the blissful savor arising through the exhilaration produced by eating and drinking, one should cultivate the state of fullness; from that, great bliss comes about.
intent_summary: Transform the pleasurable expansion felt in sensory enjoyment into contemplative fullness and thereby enter great bliss.
beginner_explanation: Pleasure from food or drink usually keeps people focused on the object. Here the practice is different: notice the spreading feeling of satisfaction and fullness in yourself. Stay with that inner glow rather than the taste, and it can open into a much deeper happiness.
scholar_explanation: The verse points to ullāsa-rasa-ānanda-vijṛmbhaṇa, the unfolding of bliss in ordinary enjoyment. Bhairava redirects attention from viṣaya to the bhṛta-avasthā or filled condition of consciousness that appears when grasping momentarily relaxes. This is a classic tantric reversal in which bhoga becomes a gateway to mahānanda when the affective expansion is recognized as cid-ānanda.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Becoming One with the Taste of Experience
sanskrit:
वगतावदविषयास्वादासमसौख्यैकतात्मन् ।
योवगनस्तन्मयत्वेन मनोरूढेस् तदात्मता ॥ ७३ ॥
translation: In the tasting of objects such as song and the like, when there is a single essence of unsurpassed pleasure, for the yogin, through becoming one with that, when the mind is mounted there, there is identity with That.
intent_summary: In moments of refined aesthetic enjoyment, merge fully with the felt essence of delight until the mind becomes identical with the deeper reality it reveals.
beginner_explanation: Music, beauty, or other pleasing experiences can sometimes absorb you completely. This verse says to notice that total absorbed enjoyment and become one with it, instead of standing apart and thinking about it. When the mind fully rests in that experience, it can reveal a deeper self beyond ordinary thinking.
scholar_explanation: Gītādi-viṣayāsvāda here refers especially to aesthetic relish, where the mind becomes briefly ekatātman with a field of enjoyment. The key is tanmayatva: not conceptual interpretation of the object, but identity with the undivided savor in which mental fluctuation subsides. In Kashmir Śaiva terms, this resembles the transmutation of rasa into recognition (pratyabhijñā) of tadātmatā, identity with Bhairava-consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Meditating Wherever the Mind Finds Contentment
sanskrit:
यि यि मनस्तुवष्टमधनस्तिैि धारयेत् ।
ति ति ऩरानन्दस्वारूऩं सम्प्रितधते ॥ ७४ ॥
translation: Wherever, wherever the mind finds satisfaction, there, there one should hold it. In that very place, the nature of supreme bliss increasingly unfolds.
intent_summary: Stabilize attention at any point where genuine mental contentment appears, because supreme bliss can reveal itself there.
beginner_explanation: If your mind naturally becomes quiet and happy somewhere, with a sound, place, feeling, or simple moment, stay there. You do not need to force a special spiritual experience. This verse teaches that deep peace can open right where the mind feels naturally content.
scholar_explanation: This is a remarkably universal dhāraṇā: tuṣṭi itself becomes the support. The instruction dhārayet indicates sustained contemplative holding at the locus where manas settles without agitation, allowing parānanda-svarūpa to manifest progressively. It resonates with the non-dual Śaiva insight that any adequately attended moment of repose may disclose the bliss-nature of consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: The Liminal State Before Sleep
sanskrit:
अनागतायां वनद्रायां प्रणष्टे िाह्यगोचरे ।
सािस्था मनसा गम्या ऩरा देिी प्रकाशते ॥ ७५ ॥
translation: When sleep has not yet arrived and the external field of perception has vanished, that state is accessible to the mind; there the supreme Goddess shines forth.
intent_summary: Attend to the threshold just before sleep, when outer perception fades but sleep has not yet fully come, and recognize the luminous inner state there.
beginner_explanation: There is a special moment before sleep when the world drops away, but you are not fully asleep yet. This verse says that if you notice that moment carefully, a subtle inner clarity can appear. It is a quiet doorway hidden inside ordinary nightly experience.
scholar_explanation: The verse identifies the nidrā-pūrvāvasthā, the hypnagogic interval in which bāhya-gocara is lost while awareness has not yet collapsed into unconscious sleep. This liminal state is 'reachable by the mind' only insofar as refined attention remains present, revealing Parā Devī as the inner luminosity of consciousness. It parallels other VBT threshold practices exploiting transitional states (sandhi) as openings into the non-dual ground.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Gazing into Luminous Sky
sanskrit:
तेजसा सूयधदीऩादेराकाशे शिऱीकृते ।
दृवष्टवनधिेश्या तिैि स्वात्मरूऩं प्रकाशते ॥ ७६ ॥
translation: When the sky is made variegated or streaked by the light of the sun, a lamp, and so on, fixing the gaze there, one's own true nature shines forth in that very place.
intent_summary: Steady the gaze in illuminated space until the radiance of one's own Self becomes evident.
beginner_explanation: If you look into space lit by sunlight, a flame, or other bright light, the open field can become strangely vivid. This verse says to keep your gaze there steadily and let the mind become quiet. In that open brightness, a deeper sense of your own being may reveal itself.
scholar_explanation: The practice uses ākāśa visually transformed by tejas—solar or lamplight—as a contemplative support. Through dṛṣṭi-niveśa in luminous space, ordinary visual cognition loosens and svātma-rūpa-prakāśa emerges, suggesting the identity of external light and the prakāśa of consciousness. The verse stands near related Śaiva and tantric uses of outer luminosity as a gateway to cid-ākāśa.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Fierce Gaze of Bhairavī
sanskrit:
करवङ्कण्या क्रोधनया भैरव्या ऱेवऱहानया ।
खेचयाध दृवष्टकाऱे च ऩरािावप्त् प्रकाशते ॥ ७७ ॥
translation: At the time of seeing the dark one, the wrathful one, Bhairavī, with lolling tongue, or Khecarī, supreme attainment shines forth.
intent_summary: Use the intense vision of a fierce goddess form as a shock-like focus through which supreme realization can flash forth.
beginner_explanation: Some spiritual images are not gentle; they are fierce, wild, even frightening. This verse says that if such a form is truly seen with steady attention, it can break ordinary mental habits and reveal something beyond fear. The point is not horror, but a sudden opening through intensity.
scholar_explanation: The verse invokes kruddhā, Bhairavī, lelihānā, and Khecarī—fierce śakti-forms whose visionary force interrupts habitual cognition. Such imagery functions as an āveśa-producing support, where the charged icon becomes a portal to parā-prāpti. In Trika symbolism, the terrifying goddess is not other than consciousness-power (śakti) in its uncontracted, transgressive revelatory mode.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Unsupported Limbs on a Soft Seat
sanskrit:
मृद्वासने विजैकेन हस्तऩादौ वनराश्रयम् ।
वनधाय तत्प्रसङ्गेन ऩरा ऩूणाध मवतभधिेत् ॥ ७८ ॥
translation: On a soft seat, with only one buttock resting, placing the hands and feet without support, by connection with that, the awareness becomes supremely full.
intent_summary: Adopt a subtly unstable bodily posture so that heightened attention leads the mind into a sense of complete fullness.
beginner_explanation: This practice uses balance and slight instability. Sitting softly with the body not fully supported makes you naturally alert, because you cannot slump into dullness. That alert, gathered feeling can turn into a strong sense of inner wholeness.
scholar_explanation: The instruction seems to prescribe an asymmetrical āsana in which support is minimized, producing heightened somatic vigilance. The phrase tat-prasaṅgena suggests that through sustained contact with this unsupported embodied condition, mati becomes parā pūrṇā—expanded into full awareness. Such body-based dhāraṇās are characteristic of the VBT's use of proprioceptive thresholds as vehicles of non-conceptual integration.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Armpit Pressure and Mental Dissolution
sanskrit:
उऩविश्यासने सम्यविाहू कृत्वाधधकुवञ्चतौ ।
कऺव्योवि मन् कुिधन् शममायावत तल्लयात् ॥ ७९ ॥
translation: Having sat properly in a seat, making the arms well bent, and contracting them, performing pressure in the region of the armpits, the mind comes to peace through dissolution into That.
intent_summary: Use a specific bodily compression posture to quiet the mind and bring it into dissolution.
beginner_explanation: Certain body positions can change the state of the mind very quickly. This verse describes a posture using bent arms and pressure near the armpits, which helps gather and calm inner energy. When the body becomes still and focused in this way, the mind can settle deeply.
scholar_explanation: This is a somatic mudrā-like dhāraṇā: bodily configuration induces śama of mind. The axillary pressure and arm contraction likely alter prāṇic flow, though the verse emphasizes the result rather than physiology: manas becomes pacified and enters laya. As elsewhere in the VBT, corporeal manipulation is employed not for haṭha-yogic ends alone but as a direct means to absorption in the non-dual ground.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Steady Gaze on a Gross Form
sanskrit:
स्थूऱरूऩस्य भािस्य स्तब्धां दृवष्टं वनऩात्य च ।
अवचरेण वनराधारं मन् कृत्वा वशिं व्रजेत् ॥ ८० ॥
translation: Casting a motionless gaze upon a gross object or form, and in a short time making the mind supportless, one attains Śiva.
intent_summary: Fix the gaze steadily on a visible object until the mind loses its dependence on supports and enters the state of Śiva.
beginner_explanation: Choose a simple visible object and look at it without shifting your eyes. As your attention becomes very steady, the usual stream of thoughts begins to thin out. Then even the object can drop away, leaving a quiet, open awareness.
scholar_explanation: This is a classic dṛṣṭi-based dhāraṇā beginning from sthūla-rūpa, a gross perceptual support. The crucial move is from visual fixation to nirādhāra-manas, the supportless mind in which object-dependence collapses and Śiva is realized. It exemplifies the tantric progression from ālambana to anālambana, from support to the non-conceptual ground of consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Awareness at the Palate Center
sanskrit:
मध्यवजह्वे िावरतास्ये मध्ये वनवऺप्य चेतनाम् ।
होच्चारं मनसा कुिंस्तत् शान्ते प्रऱीयते ॥ ८१ ॥
translation: Placing awareness in the middle of the tongue and within the mouth, and mentally performing the syllabic utterance (uccāra), one dissolves into peace.
intent_summary: The verse teaches the practitioner to rest consciousness in the oral-palatal center and use subtle inner sound to enter absorption in inner stillness.
beginner_explanation: Bring your attention to the inside of the mouth, especially the middle area near the tongue and palate. Then softly repeat a subtle inner sound in the mind, without speaking aloud. If attention becomes steady there, the mind can settle into a quiet, peaceful state.
scholar_explanation: This dhāraṇā uses the jihvā/tālu-madhya region as a subtle support for cetanā and combines it with mānasa uccāra, an interiorized phonemic ascent. The term uccāra in Trika often indicates not mere recitation but the vibratory emergence and reabsorption of consciousness through sound. The culmination in śānti suggests laya into the quiescent ground beyond articulated vikalpa.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Contemplation of the Unsupported Body
sanskrit:
आसने शयने वस्थत्वा वनराधारं विभाियन् ।
स्वदेहं मनवस वऺणे ऺणात्क्षीणाशयो भिेत् ॥ ८२ ॥
translation: Whether seated or lying down, contemplating the body as without support (nirādhāra), and dissolving one's own body in the mind, one quickly becomes one whose latent tendencies are exhausted.
intent_summary: The verse instructs the practitioner to imagine the body as groundless and mentally dissolved, weakening deep mental conditioning.
beginner_explanation: Sit or lie down and feel as if your body is not being held up by anything. Then let the sense of the body fade in the mind, as if it were melting into space. This can loosen old habits and the usual tight grip of identity.
scholar_explanation: The key term nirādhāra points to the unsupported nature of embodied appearance when stripped of conceptual fixation. To place the deha into the mind and let it attenuate is to reverse the ordinary assumption that mind is contained by body; instead body is recognized as a mental projection within consciousness. Kṣīṇāśaya indicates attenuation of latent saṃskāric deposits, a recurrent marker of entry into non-conceptual absorption.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Stillness After Gentle Body Movement
sanskrit:
चऱासने वस्थतस्याथ शनैिाध देहचाऱनात् ।
प्रशान्ते मानसे भािे देवि वदव्यौघम् आप्नुयात् ॥ ८३ ॥
translation: When one is seated on a moving seat, or after gradually inducing movement of the body, then, when the mental state becomes peaceful, O Goddess, one attains the divine flood.
intent_summary: The verse teaches using gentle bodily motion and the stillness that follows it as a gateway to an influx of expanded consciousness.
beginner_explanation: Sometimes after the body moves, a natural stillness appears on its own. This practice says to notice that quiet settling after gentle motion, like the calm after rocking stops. In that pause, the mind may open into a deeper, more vivid awareness.
scholar_explanation: The dhāraṇā exploits vestibular and proprioceptive perturbation: calāsana or deha-cālana produces a shift in sensory organization, after which praśānta mānasa-bhāva can spontaneously emerge. The promised divyaugha, 'divine torrent' or influx, evokes śaktipāta-like descent or the upsurge of expanded consciousness once ordinary sensorimotor fixation is interrupted. This aligns with VBT methods that use transitional thresholds rather than static concentration alone.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Gazing into the Stainless Sky
sanskrit:
आकाशं विमऱं ऩश्यन्कृत्वा दृवष्टं वनरन्तराम् ।
स्तब्धात्मा तत्क्षणाद्देवि भैरिं िऩुराप्नुयात् ॥ ८४ ॥
translation: Gazing continuously at the clear, stainless sky, with the self made motionless, O Goddess, one instantly attains the form of Bhairava.
intent_summary: The verse teaches uninterrupted sky-gazing and inner stillness as a direct means to expansive recognition of Bhairava-consciousness.
beginner_explanation: Look into a clear open sky without constantly shifting your gaze. Let your body and mind become very still, as if nothing needs to be done. The openness outside can help reveal a matching openness inside.
scholar_explanation: The vimala ākāśa functions as an outer analogue of cidākāśa, the pure expanse of consciousness. Nirantara dṛṣṭi and stabdhātman together suspend habitual mental fluctuation, allowing the practitioner to recognize Bhairava-vapuḥ not as an external deity-form but as one's own unbounded awareness. This method resonates with Trika uses of spatial vastness as a support for non-objective recognition (pratyabhijñā).

speaker: Bhairava
title: All Space as Bhairava
sanskrit:
ऱीनं मूवनध वियत्सिधम् भैरित्वेन भाियेत् ।
तत्सिधम् भैरिाकारतेजस्तत्त्वं समाविशेत् ॥ ८५ ॥
translation: One should contemplate the entire expanse of space, absorbed above the head, as Bhairava. Then one enters the reality of the radiant essence whose form is that all-pervasive Bhairava.
intent_summary: The verse teaches expanding contemplation into total space and recognizing that vastness itself as the radiant reality of Bhairava.
beginner_explanation: Instead of feeling awareness trapped inside the body, imagine the whole surrounding space as alive and sacred. Let that vastness be felt as one living presence rather than many separate things. By doing this, the sense of being a small isolated self can open into a more luminous unity.
scholar_explanation: Though the text is somewhat corrupt, the sense is clear: the viyat-sarvam, the whole field of space, is to be bhāvita as Bhairavatva. This is not symbolic projection but ontological recognition that the all-pervasive spatial continuum is a manifestation of Bhairava's prakāśa. Entry into bhairavākāra-tejas-tattva marks transition from conceptual contemplation to immersion in the luminous essence of non-dual consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Beyond the Duality-Creating Outer Light
sanskrit:
वकवञ्चज्ज्ञातम् द्वैतदावय िाह्याऱोकस्तम् ऩुन् ।
विश्वावद भैरिं रूऩं ऻात्वानन्तप्रकाशभृत् ॥ ८६ ॥
translation: Whatever little is known is a giver of duality; outer light indeed is that. But having known the form of Bhairava as the source of the universe, one becomes the bearer of infinite light.
intent_summary: The verse points beyond limited object-based knowing and sensory illumination toward the infinite light of Bhairava underlying all manifestation.
beginner_explanation: What we usually know comes through contrast: this and that, inner and outer, self and world. This verse says that such ordinary knowing is limited. If you recognize the deeper source behind everything, awareness is felt as boundless light rather than divided experience.
scholar_explanation: The verse contrasts kiñcid-jñāta, fragmentary object-knowledge, with the ananta-prakāśa of Bhairava, the universal ground of manifestation (viśvādi-rūpa). Bāhyāloka here signifies empirical illumination bound to subject-object structuring; it 'gives duality' because it discloses differentiated objects. Recognition of Bhairava as the luminous source shifts cognition from prameya-fragmentation to the self-revelatory prakāśa-vimarśa of non-dual consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Meditation on Darkness in the Dark Fortnight
sanskrit:
एिमेि दुवनधशायां कृष्णऩऺागमे वचरम् ।
तैवमरं भाियन् रूऩं भैरिं रूऩमेष्यवत ॥ ८७ ॥
translation: Likewise, in a moonless night during the dark half of the month, contemplating darkness for a long time, one comes to assume the form of Bhairava.
intent_summary: The verse teaches sustained contemplation of external darkness as a doorway to identification with Bhairava-consciousness.
beginner_explanation: Sit with darkness and really stay with it, especially when the night is deeply dark. Instead of fearing the absence of visible things, relax into it. What first seems empty can become full of presence.
scholar_explanation: This practice in kṛṣṇapakṣa and deep night uses tamisra not merely as visual absence but as an apophatic support that deprives the mind of differentiated form. Prolonged bhāvanā of darkness can collapse object-constructs and reveal the formless Bhairava-rūpa underlying cognition. It is structurally parallel to sky-gazing, but here the medium is unlit void rather than luminous openness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Entering the Dark Field Behind Closed Eyes
sanskrit:
एिमेि वनमील्यादौ नेिे कृष्णाभमाग्रत् ।
प्रसायध भैरिं रूऩं भाियम्स्तन्मयो भिेत् ॥ ८८ ॥
translation: In the same way, at the beginning, closing the eyes and seeing the dark mass before oneself, one should contemplate the form of Bhairava; by that, one becomes of that nature.
intent_summary: The verse teaches using the inner darkness seen behind closed eyes as a support for becoming absorbed in Bhairava.
beginner_explanation: Close your eyes and notice the dark field that appears. Instead of ignoring it, let it become the whole focus of attention. If you stay with it gently, that inner darkness can open into a sense of deep presence.
scholar_explanation: The kṛṣṇābha or dark appearance before closed eyes is treated as an immediately available inner support, analogous to external night-darkness but interiorized. Bhairava-rūpa is to be bhāvita within that undifferentiated field until tanmayatā, complete identification, arises. This is a classic VBT strategy: convert a mundane perceptual substrate into a portal to non-dual recognition.

speaker: Bhairava
title: The Gap After Sense Interruption
sanskrit:
यस्य कस्येवन्द्रयस्यावऩ व्याघाताच्च वनरोधत् ।
प्रविष्टस्याद्वये शून्ये तिैिात्मा प्रकाशते ॥ ८९ ॥
translation: Through the obstruction or cessation of any one of the senses, when one enters the non-dual void, there itself the Self shines forth.
intent_summary: The verse teaches that when a sensory channel is interrupted and attention enters the resulting gap, the radiant Self becomes evident.
beginner_explanation: If one sense suddenly stops or is cut off, there can be a brief gap before the mind fills it in again. This verse says to notice that gap. In that pause, awareness can reveal itself very directly.
scholar_explanation: Vyāghāta and nirodha of any indriya create a rupture in ordinary perceptual continuity, exposing an advaya śūnya. This 'void' is not nihilistic absence but the de-objectified field in which ātman self-manifests as prakāśa. The method aligns with Trika's frequent use of sandhi, the interval or break, as the privileged locus of recognition.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Japa of the Unpointed, Unaspirated A
sanskrit:
अविन्दुम् अविसगधम् च अकारम् जऩतो महान् ।
उदेवत देवि सहसा ऻानौघ् ऩरमेश्वर् ॥ ९० ॥
translation: By repeating the great letter 'A'—without bindu and without visarga—O Goddess, there suddenly arises a flood of knowledge, the Supreme Lord.
intent_summary: The verse teaches that meditative repetition of the pure primordial vowel A can abruptly awaken a surge of liberating knowledge.
beginner_explanation: This practice uses a very simple sound: 'A,' the open basic vowel. Repeat it inwardly and simply, without adding anything extra to it. The verse says that this pure sound can suddenly open a powerful clarity.
scholar_explanation: Akāra, devoid of bindu and visarga, signifies the unmodified phonemic ground prior to differentiation into emanative and reabsorptive phases. In Śaiva mantra-śāstra, 'A' is often the primordial matrix of all varṇa-s and a marker of anuttara, the unsurpassable. Japa here is less devotional repetition than contemplative attunement to the pure vibratory source from which jñānaugha, the torrent of gnosis identified with Parameśvara, suddenly emerges.

speaker: Bhairava
title: From Sound with Visarga to the Soundless End
sanskrit:
िणधस्य सविसगधस्य विसगाधन्तं वचवतं कुरु ।
वनराधारेण वचत्तेन स्पृशेद्ब्रह्म सनातनम् ॥ ९१ ॥
translation: Make the utterance of a syllable together with visarga and then without visarga; by relying on that uttered sound, one should touch the eternal Brahman.
intent_summary: Use the subtle transition between sounded expression and its fading termination to enter the timeless absolute.
beginner_explanation: This verse suggests listening very carefully to how a sound ends. You may chant a syllable with a soft breathy release, then notice the moment when the sound disappears. That fading edge is used as a doorway into deep stillness.
scholar_explanation: The verse hinges on savisarga and visargānta, the phonetic and energetic dynamics of emission and cessation. In Trika practice, śabda is not merely acoustic but a manifestation of spanda; attending to the terminal point of articulated vibration becomes a means of contacting sanātana brahman. It aligns with other VBT sound-based dhāraṇās in which the end of nāda reveals the unstruck ground.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Meditating on the Self as Sky-Filled Radiance
sanskrit:
व्योमाकारं स्वमात्मानम् ध्यायेवद्दवग्भरनािृतम् ।
वनराश्रया वचवत् शवि् स्वरूऩं दशधयेत्तदा ॥ ९२ ॥
translation: One should meditate on one's own Self as sky-like, filled with all directions. Then, by taking support in that expanse, one would reveal the very nature of Śiva.
intent_summary: Contemplate the Self as boundless space so that one’s identity opens into Śiva’s all-pervading nature.
beginner_explanation: Imagine your inner sense of self not as a small person inside the body, but as open space. Let that openness spread in every direction, with no hard edge anywhere. Resting in that vastness can loosen the feeling of being limited and separate.
scholar_explanation: The key image is vyomākāra ātman, the Self in the form of ākāśa, here not inert emptiness but conscious expanse. The support (āśraya) of spatial infinitude functions as a direct upāya for recognizing Śiva-svarūpa, resonant with cidākāśa contemplations in non-dual Śaivism. This verse bridges spatial visualization and ontological recognition.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Piercing Sensation with a Sharp Point
sanskrit:
वकंवचदङ्गम् विवभद्यादौ तीक्ष्णसूच्यावदना तत् ।
तिैि चेतनां युक्त्वा भैरिे वनमधऱा गवत् ॥ ९३ ॥
translation: At the beginning, one should pierce some limb with a sharp needle or the like. Joining awareness there, Bhairava-state is attained through that stainless movement.
intent_summary: Focus unwaveringly on a sharp bodily sensation until awareness disengages from ordinary mental distraction and opens into Bhairava.
beginner_explanation: This verse uses a very intense method: place attention on a strong, precise physical sensation. The point is not self-harm for its own sake, but using a vivid sensation to gather the mind completely in one place. When attention becomes total, ordinary mental chatter can suddenly drop away.
scholar_explanation: The practice works through ekāgratā generated by tīvrasparśa, here exemplified by the prick of a needle. By uniting caitanya with the locus of sensation, scattered vikalpa is suspended and awareness may flash into the nirvikalpa Bhairava-state. As in other Trika methods, an extreme sensory event is transmuted into upāya rather than rejected.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Seeing Thought-Constructs as Beginningless and Groundless
sanskrit:
वचत्ताद्यन्त्कृवतनाधवस्त ममान्तभाधियेवदवत ।
विकल्पानामभािेन विकल्पैरुवितो भिेत् ॥ ९४ ॥
translation: One should contemplate: 'Mental constructs, from beginning to end, have no real foundation in me, in the inner Self.' By the absence of conceptualization, one becomes elevated beyond conceptual constructs.
intent_summary: Recognize that thoughts have no true basis in the Self, and through this insight become free of their hold.
beginner_explanation: Thoughts seem solid because we keep believing them. This verse says to look closely and notice that thoughts do not have a firm root in your deepest self. As you stop feeding them, the mind becomes quieter and more open.
scholar_explanation: The verse directs inquiry into vikalpa as lacking substantive status within the innermost subject. By discerning their unsupported and adventitious nature, one enters avikalpa or nirvikalpa awareness, a central epistemic and soteriological pivot in Pratyabhijñā-oriented Śaivism. The movement is not suppression but ontological devaluation of conceptual proliferation.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Discerning Māyā as the Principle of Differentiation
sanskrit:
माया विमोवहनी नाम कऱाया् कऱनं वस्थतम् ।
इत्यावदधमं तत्त्वानां कऱयन्न ऩृथग्भिेत् ॥ ९५ ॥
translation: Māyā, called the deluding power, consists in the operation of kalā's measuring and division. Thus, by contemplating the principles (tattvas) in this way, one does not remain separate.
intent_summary: Understand differentiation as Māyā’s limiting activity, and through insight into the tattvas transcend the sense of separateness.
beginner_explanation: This verse says separation is produced by a power that divides reality into pieces. When you understand that this dividing tendency is not the deepest truth, you begin to see unity beneath apparent differences. The practice is a shift in how you understand experience.
scholar_explanation: Māyā here is not mere illusion in a simplistic sense but the tattvic power of differentiation, linked with kalā and limitation. To 'contemplate the tattvas' is to understand the architecture of manifestation without reifying difference; such discernment dissolves pṛthagbhāva, the sense of separateness. This is deeply consonant with the Trika reading of bondage as contracted self-apprehension.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Tracing Desire Back to Its Source
sanskrit:
झवगतीच्छां समुत्पन्नामिऱोक्य शमं नयेत् ।
यत एि समुद्भूता ततस्तिैि ऱीयते ॥ ९६ ॥
translation: When a surge of desire arises, one should observe it and bring it to शांति (peace). From wherever it has arisen, there itself it dissolves.
intent_summary: Watch desire at the moment of its arising and let it subside back into its source.
beginner_explanation: Instead of chasing a desire or fighting it, simply notice it very early. Look at where it comes from in your mind or being. If you stay with it calmly, it can sink back into that same place by itself.
scholar_explanation: The verse presents icchā not as a moral problem but as an energetic emergence to be observed at its udbhava. By sustained non-reactive attention, the vṛtti returns to its source, revealing laya in the very locus of arising. This mirrors Trika's broader strategy of using manifested śakti as the path back to its own ground.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Who Am I Before Will or Knowledge Arise?
sanskrit:
यदा ममेच्छा नोत्पन्ना ऻानं िा कस्तदावस्म िै ।
तत्त्वतोऽहम् तथाभूतस्तल्लीनस्तन्मना भिेत् ॥ ९७ ॥
translation: When no desire has arisen in me, nor any knowledge—what indeed am I then? In truth, being thus, one should become absorbed in That, with mind made of That.
intent_summary: Investigate the state prior to the arising of will and cognition, and merge into that fundamental identity.
beginner_explanation: Before a thought, intention, or piece of knowledge appears, there is still a basic sense of being. This verse asks you to notice that simple 'I am' before mental activity starts. Resting there can reveal a deeper identity beyond the usual mind.
scholar_explanation: The inquiry targets the pre-conceptual interval prior to icchā and jñāna, disclosing the aham in its less contracted mode. The instruction to become tanmaya and tallīna indicates absorption into the foundational subjectivity that precedes determinate cognition. It strongly reflects the Pratyabhijñā emphasis on recognizing the primordial I-consciousness beneath mental functions.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Entering the Moment of Desire or Knowing
sanskrit:
इच्छायामथिा ऻाने जाते वचत्तं वनिेशयेत् ।
आत्मिुद्ध्यानन्यचेतास्ततस्तत्त्वाथधदशधनम् ॥ ९८ ॥
translation: At the arising of desire or of knowledge, one should place the mind there. With the understanding of the Self and with undivided awareness, then the vision of reality's meaning appears.
intent_summary: Fix awareness directly in the instant desire or cognition arises, and through non-dual self-awareness realize the truth of reality.
beginner_explanation: When wanting or knowing suddenly appears, catch that very moment. Instead of following the content, notice the energy of its appearance itself. That shift can reveal a deeper clarity underneath the mind's movements.
scholar_explanation: This verse complements the previous one: rather than examining the prior gap, it uses the very birth of icchā or jñāna as the meditative locus. Through ātma-buddhi and ananya-cetas, the practitioner recognizes tattvārtha-darśana—the real significance of phenomena as expressions of consciousness. It is a classic Trika transmutation of mental emergence into revelatory awareness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Knowledge Without Cause or Support is Delusive
sanskrit:
वनवनधवमत्तं भिेज्ज्ञानम् वनराधारं भ्रमात्मकम् ।
तत्त्वत् कस्यवचन्नैतद् एिम्भािी वशि् वप्रये ॥ ९९ ॥
translation: Knowledge that appears without distinct cause, without support, is of the nature of भ्रम (delusion). In truth, it belongs to no one whatsoever. One who understands thus becomes Śiva, O Beloved.
intent_summary: Discern unsupported and ownerless cognition as insubstantial, and through that insight awaken to Śiva-nature.
beginner_explanation: Sometimes thoughts or impressions just appear, and we quickly assume, 'This is mine' or 'This is true.' This verse says to notice that such mental events may have no solid basis and do not really belong to a separate self. Seeing that clearly can free you from being trapped by them.
scholar_explanation: The verse deconstructs jñāna as an apparently autonomous event lacking fixed nimitta or ādhāra, exposing its bhramātmaka status when appropriated by egoic ownership. Realization that cognition is not truly 'someone's' undermines limited subjecthood and opens śiva-bhāva. This intersects with non-dual Śaiva critiques of contracted pramātṛ-identity.

speaker: Bhairava
title: One Conscious Dharma in All Bodies
sanskrit:
वचद्धमाध सिधदेहेषु विशेषो नावस्त कुिवचत् ।
अतश्च तन्मयं सिं भाियन्भिवजज्जन् ॥ १०० ॥
translation: The nature of consciousness exists in all bodies; there is no distinction anywhere. Therefore, contemplating everything as consisting of That, one becomes Bhairava-like.
intent_summary: See the same consciousness equally present in all beings and all forms, and thereby realize Bhairava.
beginner_explanation: This verse says the same awareness lives in everyone, not different kinds of awareness in different bodies. If you reflect deeply that all beings share one conscious essence, the sense of separation softens. The practice is to see unity where we usually see many separate lives.
scholar_explanation: Cid-dharma is declared universal across all embodied forms, denying any ultimate viśeṣa among conscious beings. The contemplation of sarvaṃ tanmayam is a direct non-dual expansion from individual consciousness to Bhairava-consciousness. This is fully aligned with Trika's recognition that the one cit manifests as all pramātṛs and objects alike.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Transcending the Passions by Objectless Awareness
sanskrit:
कामक्रोधऱोभमोहमदमात्सयधगोचरे ।
िुवद्धं वनवस्तवमतां कृत्वा तत्तत्त्वमिवशष्यते ॥ १०१ ॥
translation: In the field of desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy, making the mind supportless and without fixation on any object, that reality-principle alone remains.
intent_summary: The verse teaches the practitioner to release mental support even amidst strong passions so that the underlying reality alone is revealed.
beginner_explanation: Usually, strong emotions pull the mind outward toward some story or object. This verse says that in the middle of such states, if you do not cling to what the emotion is about, something deeper remains. That deeper stillness is the point of the practice.
scholar_explanation: The list kāma-krodha-lobha-moha-mada-mātsarya names the classic afflictive states, but the method is not moral suppression; it is nirālambatā, making awareness unsupported by viṣaya. When vṛtti is deprived of its object-basis even in the midst of kleśic activation, tattva alone 'remains' (avaśiṣyate), indicating recognition of the substratum beyond reactive mentation. The verse aligns with the VBT strategy of using charged states as entry points into laya and Bhairava-consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Contemplating the World as Magical Illusion
sanskrit:
इन्द्रजाऱमयं विश्वं व्यस्तं िा वचिकमधित् ।
भ्रमद्वा ध्यायत् सिं ऩश्यतश्च सुखोद्गम् ॥ १०२ ॥
translation: This universe is made of Indra's net, dispersed as though a magical display. Meditating on it thus, or seeing it as a whirling illusion, one experiences an upsurge of bliss.
intent_summary: The verse instructs one to contemplate the world as an illusory magical display in order to loosen fixation and open into bliss.
beginner_explanation: Think of the world as a kind of moving appearance, like a magician's show or a shimmering web. When you stop treating everything as heavy and solid, the mind relaxes. From that loosening, a natural joy can arise.
scholar_explanation: The imagery of indrajāla evokes both magical illusion and interwoven manifestation, while bhrama suggests unstable, turning appearance. The practice is not crude nihilism but a phenomenological de-solidification of the world-process, weakening reified prameya-status. Sukhodgama, the arising of bliss, follows when cognition ceases to grip the universe as absolutely separate or substantial.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Abiding in the Middle Beyond Pleasure and Pain
sanskrit:
न वचत्तं वनवऺऩेद् दु्खे न सुखे िा ऩवरवऺऩेत् ।
भैरवि ऻायतां मध्ये वकं तत्त्वमिवशष्यते ॥ १०३ ॥
translation: One should not cast the mind into sorrow, nor should one throw it into pleasure. O Bhairavi, let one know the middle; what reality-principle remains there?
intent_summary: The verse teaches resting in the middle state between attraction and aversion to discover the underlying reality.
beginner_explanation: When something painful happens, we usually sink into it; when something pleasant happens, we rush toward it. This verse advises neither move. Stay balanced in the middle and notice what is present before reaction takes over.
scholar_explanation: The 'middle' (madhya) here is the crucial Kaula and Trika locus where dual movements of duḥkha and sukha, aversion and grasping, are suspended. Rather than oscillating between hedonic poles, awareness attends to the interval prior to affective appropriation. The inquiry 'what remains?' points to the residue-free ground of consciousness disclosed when mental projection into opposites ceases.

speaker: Bhairava
title: I Am All: Expanding Beyond the Body
sanskrit:
विहाय वनजदेहस्थं सिधिास्मीवत भाियन् ।
दृढेन मनसा दृष्ट्या नान्येवऺण्या सुखी भिेत् ॥ १०४ ॥
translation: Abandoning identification with one's own body and contemplating 'I am all,' with firm mind and vision not directed elsewhere, one becomes happy.
intent_summary: The verse instructs the practitioner to drop body-limitation and stabilize in the expansive recognition 'I am all.'
beginner_explanation: Most of the time, we feel that we are only this body. This practice asks you to let go of that narrow feeling and deeply sense, 'I am not limited; I am the whole.' Holding that steadily brings a wide and peaceful happiness.
scholar_explanation: The phrase sarvāsmīti bhāvayan points to universalized aham-vimarśa, the expansion of self-awareness beyond deha-pariccheda. 'With firm mind and sight' suggests resolute, non-distracted abidance rather than imaginative inflation. The verse reflects the Trika movement from contracted embodiment to the recognition of oneself as the all-pervading subject, a practical entry into śivavyāpti.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Seeing Awareness in Pot and Self as All-Pervading
sanskrit:
घटादौ यच्च विऻानवमच्छाद्यं िा ममान्तरे ।
नैि सिधगतं जातं भाियवन्नवत सिधग् ॥ १०५ ॥
translation: That consciousness which appears in a pot or other object, and also within me—contemplating it as not arising separately but as all-pervading, one becomes all-pervading.
intent_summary: The verse teaches one to recognize the same consciousness in external objects and within oneself, and thereby realize all-pervasiveness.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that the awareness by which you know an object and the awareness you feel as 'inside me' are not two different things. If you keep reflecting in this way, the sense of being trapped inside a small personal bubble begins to dissolve. You start to feel open and spacious.
scholar_explanation: The contrast between ghaṭa-ādi and mama-antare invokes a classic epistemic polarity: object-side appearance and inner subjectivity. The practice collapses this distinction by seeing vijñāna not as discretely generated in here and there, but as sarvagata, universally present. The fruit 'one becomes all-pervading' indicates assimilation to the nature of consciousness as vyāpin rather than localized knowerhood.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Attentiveness to the Knower-Known Relation
sanskrit:
ग्राह्यग्राहकसविवत्त् सामान्या सिधदेवहनाम् ।
योवगनां तु विशेषोऽवस्त सम्बन्धे सािधानता ॥ १०६ ॥
translation: The activity of the known and the knower is common to all embodied beings; but for yogins there is a distinction: careful attentiveness to the relation between them.
intent_summary: The verse teaches that yogic practice lies in closely observing the relation between subject and object rather than merely functioning within it unconsciously.
beginner_explanation: Everyone experiences a 'me' who knows and a 'thing' being known. The difference for a yogi is that they pay close attention to this process itself. By noticing how knowing happens, deeper insight opens.
scholar_explanation: Grāhya-grāhaka-saṃvitti, the cognition structured as object and subject, belongs to ordinary embodied life. The yogin's viśeṣa lies in sambandhe sāvadhānatā—precise attentiveness to the relation itself, not merely its poles. This is a characteristic VBT move: insight arises through reflexive examination of cognition, potentially revealing the nondual ground prior to pramātṛ-prameya bifurcation.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Feeling Awareness in Another Body
sanskrit:
स्विदन्यशरीरेऽवऩ सविवत्तं अनुभाियेत् ।
अऩेऺां स्वशरीरस्य त्यक्त्वा व्याऩी वदनैर् भिेत् ॥ १०७ ॥
translation: One should experience the same awareness even in another's body. Abandoning dependence upon one's own body, one becomes all-pervading within days.
intent_summary: The verse instructs the practitioner to extend felt awareness beyond their own body into others, loosening bodily exclusivity and realizing pervasion.
beginner_explanation: Normally, we feel awareness as locked inside our own skin. This practice asks you to sense consciousness in another body too, as if life is not private but shared. As this becomes natural, the sense of being limited to one body starts to soften.
scholar_explanation: The instruction to experience saṃvitti in another body radicalizes the deconstruction of dehābhimāna. By relinquishing apekṣā toward one's own body as privileged locus of subjectivity, the practitioner enters vyāpti, expansive identity beyond corporeal enclosure. This resonates with Trika's critique of contracted individuality and its affirmation of consciousness as nonlocal and transpersonal.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Making the Mind Supportless Beyond Thought
sanskrit:
वनराधारं मन् कृत्वा विकल्पान्न विकल्पयेत् ।
तदात्मऩरमात्मत्वे भैरिो मृगऱोचने ॥ १०८ ॥
translation: Making the mind supportless, one should not construct thought from thoughts. Then, in the identity of one's own Self and the Supreme Self, one becomes Bhairava, O doe-eyed one.
intent_summary: The verse teaches dissolving conceptual construction by rendering the mind supportless, leading to identity with the Supreme Self.
beginner_explanation: The mind usually keeps building one thought on top of another. This practice is to stop feeding that chain and let the mind rest without holding onto anything. In that unsupported stillness, a deeper identity is revealed.
scholar_explanation: Nirādhāraṃ manaḥ kṛtvā and vikalpān na vikalpayet succinctly describe deconstructing discursivity at its root: do not elaborate conceptualization from conceptual seeds. The fruit is tadātma-paramātmatva, the recognition that individual selfhood and supreme Self are not-two. This is a classic VBT formulation of Bhairava-realization through the cessation of vikalpa-supported mind.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Firm Recognition: I Am Shiva
sanskrit:
सिधऻ् सिधकताध च व्याऩक् ऩरमेश्वर् ।
स एिाहम् शैिधमाध इवत दार्ढ्ाधवच्छिो भिेत् ॥ १०९ ॥
translation: The omniscient, all-doing, all-pervading Supreme Lord—He indeed am I, of the nature of Shiva. By such firm conviction one becomes Shiva.
intent_summary: The verse teaches unwavering identification with the qualities of the Supreme Lord as a direct means to Shiva-realization.
beginner_explanation: This is a meditation of deep identity, not worship from a distance. Instead of thinking of the divine as somewhere else, you firmly recognize, 'That all-pervading reality is what I truly am.' Holding this steadily transforms how you experience yourself.
scholar_explanation: The verse deploys classical īśvara-attributes—sarvajña, sarvakartṛ, vyāpaka, parameśvara—not as theological predicates of a distant deity but as recognitive descriptors of the true aham. The declaration sa evāham is a concise expression of Pratyabhijñā: liberation occurs through firm recognition (dārḍhya) of one's identity with Śiva. The culmination 'one becomes Śiva' points not to production but to disclosure of an already present nature.

speaker: Bhairava
title: The Universe as Rays of Bhairava
sanskrit:
जऱस्येिोमधयो िह्नेर्ज्ाधऱाभङ्ग्य् प्रभा रिे् ।
ममैि भैरिस्यैता विश्वभङ्ग्यो विभेवदता् ॥ ११० ॥
translation: Just as rays of light belong to the sun, or flames and sparks to fire, so these differentiated forms of the universe are my own manifestations, of Bhairava.
intent_summary: The verse teaches seeing the diverse universe as nothing other than the radiant expression of Bhairava.
beginner_explanation: The many forms of the world may look separate, but this verse says they are like rays from one sun. Diversity is real as expression, but not separate at the root. Seeing this changes the world from a collection of disconnected things into one living display.
scholar_explanation: The analogies of solar rays and fiery emissions articulate bhedābheda-like manifestation within a nondual frame: apparent multiplicity is a vibrational unfolding of one source. Viśvabhaṅgyaḥ, the differentiated structures of the universe, are not external to Bhairava but His own self-expression. This is a key Trika insight: manifestation neither compromises transcendence nor establishes true separation from the absolute.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Whirling Until the Shock of Stillness
sanskrit:
भ्रान्त्वा भ्रान्त्वा शरीरेण त्ववरतम् भुवि ऩातनात् ।
ऺोभशविविरामेण ऩरा संजायते दशा ॥ १११ ॥
translation: By घूमता-घूमता (moving about, whirling) with the body, and then suddenly falling again and again upon the ground, through the cessation of the agitation-shock, a supreme state arises.
intent_summary: Use intense bodily motion followed by abrupt collapse and the settling of inner disturbance to reveal a higher state of consciousness.
beginner_explanation: This method uses strong movement to shake up your normal sense of control. When the motion stops suddenly, there can be a brief, unusual stillness before the mind reorganizes itself. The practice points to that gap. It is like stirring water hard and then noticing the instant when the surface begins to become clear.
scholar_explanation: This verse describes a kṣobha-based upāya: deliberate bodily disorientation (bhrāntvā bhrāntvā śarīreṇa) followed by abrupt interruption. The key is not the dramatic action itself but the kṣobha-śakti coming to viśrāma, where the vikalpa-structure momentarily suspends and parā daśā manifests. It parallels other VBT techniques that exploit transitional shock, interruption, or energetic arrest as portals into Bhairava-consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: At the End of Energetic Shock in the Centers
sanskrit:
आधारेष्वथिाऽशक्त्याऽऻानावच्चत्तऱयेन िा ।
जातशविसमािेशऺोभान्ते भैरिं िऩु् ॥ ११२ ॥
translation: Or, through inability (aśaktyā), through dulling as if by ignorance, or through the melting/fainting of the mind in the bodily supports (ādhāras), when the agitation of the arisen power comes to an end, the body of Bhairava appears.
intent_summary: Attend to the endpoint of energetic upheaval or mental collapse within the bodily centers, where Bhairava is revealed.
beginner_explanation: Sometimes after strain, weakness, overwhelm, or a strong inner energy shift, there is a moment when everything drops. Instead of resisting that moment, this verse says to notice it carefully. When the inner shaking ends, a deeper presence may become obvious.
scholar_explanation: The verse is textually difficult, but its logic is clear: in the ādhāras, when śakti has arisen (jāta-śakti-samāveśa) and the kṣobha reaches cessation, Bhairava-vapuḥ is disclosed. Terms such as aśakti, ajñāna-vat, and citta-laya indicate altered thresholds where ordinary cognitive structuring weakens. This belongs to the VBT’s broader phenomenology of liminal states in which weakened mental agency permits a direct manifestation of non-conceptual awareness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Steadiness in the Two Channels of Vision
sanskrit:
सम्प्रदायवममं देवि शृणु सम्यविदाम्यहम् ।
कैिल्यं जायते सद्यो नेियो् स्तब्धमाियो् ॥ ११३ ॥
translation: Hear, O Goddess, this traditional teaching as I explain it rightly: liberation (kaivalya) arises immediately when the two eyes become fixed and unmoving.
intent_summary: Stabilize the gaze completely so that mental movement stops and immediate liberation becomes accessible.
beginner_explanation: When the eyes stop darting around, the mind often becomes quieter too. This verse suggests holding the gaze very still, without strain, until a deeper calm opens. It is like letting a restless camera finally come into perfect focus.
scholar_explanation: This is presented explicitly as a sampradāya, a transmitted yogic instruction. The stilling of the two eyes (netrayoḥ stabdha-mānayoḥ) functions as a gateway to kaivalya by arresting the outward-projecting tendencies tied to perception and vikalpa. It stands close to tantric forms of dṛṣṭi-sthairya and can be read alongside śāmbhavopāya methods where minimal intervention yields immediate recognition.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Contracting the Throat and Lower Gate
sanskrit:
सम्कोचं कणधयो् कृत्वा ह्यधोद्वारे तथैि च ।
अनच्कमहऱं ध्यायविशेद्ब्रह्म सनातनम् ॥ ११४ ॥
translation: Making contraction in the kaṇḍa/region of the throat and likewise in the lower gate, one should meditate on the unmatched (anacka/anākhya), and enter the eternal Brahman.
intent_summary: Use bodily locks at upper and lower points to concentrate awareness and enter the timeless absolute.
beginner_explanation: This practice uses a physical tightening or sealing in the upper and lower parts of the body to gather scattered energy. While holding that inward pull, you focus on what cannot really be described in words. The idea is that when your energy stops leaking outward, attention can sink into something vast and timeless.
scholar_explanation: The verse points to a bandha-like procedure involving kaṇṭha and adho-dvāra, likely an upper-lower energetic sealing analogous to later haṭhayogic locks, though framed here in a nondual contemplative context. The object of meditation is the anākhya/anacchka-mahala—likely the inexpressible supreme principle beyond conceptual determination. The result is not merely subtle-energy control but entry into sanātana-brahman through concentrated containment of prāṇic flow.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Looking Down from a Great Height
sanskrit:
कूऩावदके महागते वस्थत्वोऩवर वनरीऺणात् ।
अविकल्पमते् सम्यक्सद्यवश्चत्तऱय् िुटम् ॥ ११५ ॥
translation: Standing at the edge of a well, precipice, or other great height, by looking downward from above, for one whose mind is free of conceptualization, the dissolution of mind occurs immediately and clearly.
intent_summary: Use the shock of open depth and downward vision to suspend thought and enter immediate mental dissolution.
beginner_explanation: Looking into a deep drop can create a sudden, open, thought-free feeling. This verse says to notice that raw moment instead of following fear or commentary. The depth outside can trigger a depth inside.
scholar_explanation: This is a classic VBT use of environmental vastness and vertiginous interruption. The downward gaze into depth (mahā-garta) can induce avikalpa-mati, and from that non-conceptual stance citta-laya manifests at once. The outer abyss serves as an analogue and catalyst for recognition of the inner śūnya/chid-ākāśa.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Wherever the Mind Goes, There Is Shiva
sanskrit:
यि यि मनो यावत िाह्ये िाभ्यन्तरेऽवऩ िा ।
ति ति वशिािास्था व्याऩकत्वात्क्व यास्यवत ॥ ११६ ॥
translation: Wherever the mind goes—outward or even inward—there indeed is the state of Śiva; because of His all-pervasiveness, where could it go?
intent_summary: Recognize that every movement of mind already occurs within the all-pervading reality of Shiva.
beginner_explanation: Usually we think some thoughts are spiritual and others are distractions. This verse overturns that idea by saying the mind can never leave the field of awareness. Wherever attention goes, that too is happening inside the same vast presence.
scholar_explanation: This is a succinct statement of nondual Śaiva metaphysics: whether bāhya or ābhyantara, every cognition unfolds within Śiva’s vyāpakatva. The practice is thus not suppression of mental movement but pratyabhijñā—recognition that no thought exits the expanse of consciousness. It resonates strongly with the Trika understanding that the universe is Śiva’s own vimarśa and never truly outside Him.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Tracing Consciousness Through the Senses
sanskrit:
यि यिाऺमागेण चैतन्यं व्यज्यते विभो् ।
तस्य तन्मािधवमधत्वावच्चल्लयाद्भवरतात्मता ॥ ११७ ॥
translation: Wherever, by any avenue of the senses, consciousness shines forth, O Radiant One, by contemplating that as having the nature of that very consciousness, one becomes filled with Bhairava through the dissolution of mind.
intent_summary: Notice consciousness itself as it appears through any sensory channel, and let the mind dissolve into that living awareness.
beginner_explanation: Any sight, sound, touch, taste, or smell can become a doorway. Instead of getting caught in the object, notice the fact that you are aware of it. When you turn toward the awareness shining through experience, the sense of separateness can soften.
scholar_explanation: The phrase akṣa-mārga indicates the sense pathways as loci where caitanya becomes manifest. By recognizing the object-field as non-other than that illuminating consciousness (tan-mātra-dharma), citta-laya occurs and bhairavatā—being filled with Bhairava—emerges. This is an elegant phenomenological move from viṣaya to prakāśa-vimarśa, akin to śāmbhavopāya recognition through immediate cognition.

speaker: Bhairava
title: At the Edge of Hunger, Fear, and Astonishment
sanskrit:
ऺुताद्यन्ते भये शोके गह्वरे िा रणाद्द्रुते ।
कुतूहऱेऺुधाद्यन्ते ब्रह्मसत्तामयी दशा ॥ ११८ ॥
translation: At the end of hunger and similar states, in fear, in grief, in a cavern, or while fleeing in battle; at the end of curiosity, thirst, and such states, there is a condition consisting of the reality of Brahman.
intent_summary: Recognize the naked state that appears at the climax or endpoint of intense human conditions such as hunger, fear, grief, urgency, or wonder.
beginner_explanation: Strong experiences can briefly strip away your usual mental chatter. This verse says the moments at the peak or ending of hunger, fear, shock, grief, or intense curiosity can reveal something very pure. If you stay present instead of reacting automatically, those raw moments can open into deep awareness.
scholar_explanation: A paradigmatic VBT strategy: exploit liminality at the anta of powerful affective or survival states. Whether kṣut, bhaya, śoka, kautūhala, or tṛṣṇā, the interruption of ordinary vikalpa at their threshold reveals brahma-sattā-mayī daśā. The verse belongs to a cluster using heightened psychophysical intensity not as obstruction but as a direct means of nondual disclosure.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Letting Go of Mind in Remembered and Seen Objects
sanskrit:
िस्तुषु स्मयधमाणेषु दृष्टे देशे मनस् त्यजेत् ।
स्वशरीरं वनराधारं कृत्वा प्रसरवत प्रभु् ॥ ११९ ॥
translation: While objects are being remembered, or when a place is seen, one should abandon the mind there; having made one’s own body supportless, the Lord expands forth.
intent_summary: Release mental fixation on remembered or perceived objects, and by becoming supportless allow the inner Lord to unfold.
beginner_explanation: When a memory or a visible thing grabs your attention, don't keep feeding the story around it. Let the mind drop away from the object, and feel yourself without leaning on any mental support. In that openness, a deeper sense of presence can spread on its own.
scholar_explanation: The instruction is to relinquish manas precisely in the act of smaryamāṇa or dṛṣṭa-object engagement, rather than after withdrawing from experience. Nirādhāratā of the body here signifies release from identification with embodied support-structures, allowing Prabhu—the sovereign consciousness—to prasṛ, expand. This aligns with nirālamba awareness practices central to nondual Śaiva contemplative method.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Soft Gaze Into the Void Behind Seeing
sanskrit:
क्ववचद्वस्तुवन विन्यस्य शनैदृधवष्टम् वनितधयेत् ।
तज्ज्ञानं वचत्तसवहतं देवि शून्याऱायो भिेत् ॥१२० ॥
translation: Fixing the gaze on some object, one should slowly withdraw the sight; then, O Goddess, that knowledge together with the mind becomes absorbed into the abode of emptiness (śūnya-ālaya).
intent_summary: Rest the gaze on an object and gently retract visual engagement until both knowing and mind dissolve into inner emptiness.
beginner_explanation: First look at something steadily. Then, without abruptly turning away, soften and pull back the act of looking itself. As the usual focus fades, you may notice a spacious, empty awareness behind seeing.
scholar_explanation: This verse describes a subtle dṛṣṭi-pratyāhāra: visual fixation followed by gradual nivartana of the gaze-function itself. The resulting merger of jñāna and citta into śūnyālaya marks not mere sensory withdrawal but entry into the void-ground of cognition. It is closely related to avikalpa-oriented visual methods and to the VBT’s use of perception as a gateway to the inner śūnya.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Surge of Devotion as Śāṅkarī State
sanskrit:
भक्त्युद्रेकावद्वरिस्य यादृशी जायते मवत् ।
सा शवि् शाङ्करी वनत्यं भियेत्तां तत् वशि् ॥ १२१ ॥
translation: When, through an upsurge of devotion (bhaktyudreka), a state arises like that of intoxication or overwhelming absorption, that indeed is the Śāṅkarī condition; entering into it, one comes under its power.
intent_summary: Use an intense rise of devotion as a gateway into absorption in the divine state.
beginner_explanation: Sometimes love for the divine becomes so strong that it sweeps away ordinary thinking. This verse says that such a moment is not a distraction but a doorway. Instead of pulling back, let yourself rest in that holy intensity until it carries you inward.
scholar_explanation: The verse valorizes bhaktyudreka—an eruptive intensification of devotion—as a direct means rather than a merely preparatory sentiment. The term Śāṅkarī indicates the state belonging to Śaṅkara/Bhairava-Śakti, suggesting that devotional ecstasy can function as a śāmbhava-type entry into nondual absorption. Affect here is transmuted into upāya, consistent with Trika's capacity to sacralize heightened states of consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Meditating on the Void Between Perceptions
sanskrit:
िस्त्वन्तरे िेद्यमाने सिधिस्तुषु शून्यता ।
तामेि मनसा ध्यात्वा विवदतोऽवऩ प्रशाम्यवत ॥ १२२ ॥
translation: When, between one cognition and another, there is the voidness (śūnyatā) present within the accomplishments or mental events, by meditating with the mind on that alone, the disputing mind gradually becomes pacified.
intent_summary: Notice the gap between thoughts or perceptions and meditate on that inner emptiness until mental agitation subsides.
beginner_explanation: Between two thoughts there is often a tiny pause. This verse invites you to notice that quiet gap instead of following the next thought. If you keep returning to that pause, the mind's habit of arguing and chattering begins to calm down.
scholar_explanation: The locus is the antarāla, the interval between successive vedyas or cognitions, where śūnyatā flashes forth. This is a classic VBT strategy: not suppressing vikalpa by force, but discerning the interstitial non-conceptual ground that underlies mentation. The phrase about debate or discursivity becoming pacified points to the attenuation of vikalpa-prapañca through sustained attention to the gap.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Beyond Pure and Impure
sanskrit:
वकंवचज्ज्ञैयाध स्मृता शुवद्ध् सा शुवद्ध् शम्भुदशधने ।
न शुवचह्यधशुवचस्तस्मावन्नविधकल्प् सुखी भिेत् ॥ १२३ ॥
translation: What is called purity is only a limited conception; true purity is in the attainment of the state of Śambhu. There, there is neither pure nor impure; therefore, free of conceptual alternatives, one should abide happily.
intent_summary: Go beyond mental ideas of purity and impurity by resting in the nondual state of Śambhu.
beginner_explanation: We often divide experience into clean and unclean, spiritual and unspiritual. This verse says those divisions belong to the thinking mind, not to the deepest reality. Real freedom comes when you stop getting trapped in those labels and rest in a deeper wholeness.
scholar_explanation: The verse explicitly relativizes śuddhi as ordinarily conceived, recasting genuine purity as śambhudaśā—abidance in Śambhu's state. Its rejection of the binary śuci/aśuci resonates with the nondual Kaula-Trika critique of ritual and conceptual purity when severed from recognition (pratyabhijñā). Nirvikalpatā here is not mere blankness but freedom from oppositional superimposition.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Bhairava Present in the Ordinary
sanskrit:
सिधि भैरिो भाि् सामान्येष्ववऩ गोचर् ।
न च तद्व्यवतरेिेण ऩरोऽस्तीत्यद्वया गवत् ॥ १२४ ॥
translation: This Bhairava-state is accessible even in common, ordinary experiences; and apart from that, there is no higher reality—thus is the nondual course.
intent_summary: Recognize that Bhairava is present within ordinary experience itself, not somewhere separate from it.
beginner_explanation: You do not have to escape daily life to find the sacred. This verse says the highest reality is available right in ordinary moments. The practice is to stop looking elsewhere and notice the divine within what is already happening.
scholar_explanation: The verse democratizes access to bhairavabhāva by locating it in sāmānya-gochara, the field of ordinary experience. Its second hemistich makes the doctrinal point explicit: there is no para apart from this, which is the very trajectory of advaya. This aligns closely with Pratyabhijñā's insistence that recognition occurs in and as lived cognition, not outside manifestation.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Equanimity in Friend and Foe
sanskrit:
सम् शिौ च वमिे च समो मानािमानयो् ॥
ब्रह्मण् ऩवरऩूणधत्वावदवत ऻात्वा सुखी भिेत् ॥ १२५ ॥
translation: Toward friend and enemy alike, and in honor and dishonor, one should remain the same; knowing Brahman as complete fullness (paripūrṇatva), one becomes happy.
intent_summary: Cultivate sameness amid opposites by recognizing the all-complete fullness of reality.
beginner_explanation: Usually the mind leans toward praise and friends, and recoils from blame and enemies. This verse teaches balance: try to remain steady in both pleasant and unpleasant situations. That steadiness grows from sensing that your deepest being is already full and not reduced by circumstances.
scholar_explanation: Samatā toward śatru/mitra and māna/apamāna is grounded not in ethical stoicism alone but in Brahman's paripūrṇatva, plenary completeness. This is a practical expression of nondual vision, where reactive contraction before opposites weakens as one recognizes undiminished fullness. The verse echoes broader Śaiva and Gītā-like themes while recontextualizing them within Bhairava-realization.

speaker: Bhairava
title: The Middle Beyond Attachment and Aversion
sanskrit:
न द्वेषं भाियेत्क्वावऩ न रागं भाियेत्क्ववचत् ।
रागद्वेषविवनमुधिौ मध्ये ब्रह्म प्रसऩधवत ॥ १२६ ॥
translation: One should not cultivate hatred anywhere, nor should one cultivate attachment anywhere. When attachment and aversion are released, in the middle Brahman unfolds.
intent_summary: Let go of both attraction and repulsion and discover the awakened middle that appears between them.
beginner_explanation: The mind is often pulled by liking and pushed by disliking. This verse suggests not feeding either side. When you stop getting dragged by both, a quiet open center appears, and that center is the place of freedom.
scholar_explanation: Rāga and dveṣa are here treated phenomenologically as polarizing movements that obscure the madhya. Their relinquishment reveals Brahman as prasarpati—spreading forth or shining in the middle. This accords with the centrality of madhya in Kashmir Śaivism, where liberation is often accessed through the center-point between dualistic extremes.

speaker: Bhairava
title: All Knowable Things as Bhairava
sanskrit:
यदिेद्यं यदग्राह्यं यच्छून्यं यदभािगम् ।
तत्सिं भैरिं भाव्यं तदन्ते िोधसम्भि् ॥ १२७ ॥
translation: Whatever is known, whatever is grasped, whatever is void, whatever is without apparent existence—all that should be contemplated as Bhairava; at the end of that, awakening arises.
intent_summary: Reframe every kind of experience and non-experience alike as Bhairava until insight awakens.
beginner_explanation: This verse is very radical: whatever appears, and even what seems empty or absent, treat it all as the sacred. Instead of dividing reality into spiritual and non-spiritual, include everything. When this becomes steady, a deep shift in understanding occurs.
scholar_explanation: The verse universalizes bhāvanā by extending it to jñeya, grāhya, śūnya, and even abhāvagam—presence, objecthood, voidness, and apparent absence. Such total sacralization dissolves epistemic dualism by reading every mode of appearing as Bhairava's own self-disclosure. The promised bodhasambhava marks the maturation of contemplative re-cognition into awakened insight.

speaker: Bhairava
title: From Outer Sky to Skyless Absorption
sanskrit:
वनत्ये वनराश्रये शून्ये व्याऩके कऱनोविते ।
िाह्याकाशे मन् कृत्वा वनराकाशं समाविशेत् ॥ १२८ ॥
translation: In the eternal, supportless, void, all-pervasive reality, free from divisions, fixing the mind on the outer sky, one should enter the skyless state.
intent_summary: Use contemplation of the open sky to enter the supportless inner expanse beyond even the notion of space.
beginner_explanation: Looking at the open sky can help the mind feel wide and less cramped. This verse says to use that vastness as a doorway. First rest in the sense of open space outside, then let the mind slip into an even deeper openness that has no boundary at all.
scholar_explanation: The outer ākāśa serves as an upāya for entry into nirākāśa—the trans-spatial expanse beyond objectified space. The descriptors nitya, nirāśraya, śūnya, vyāpaka, and kalanocchinna frame this as the undivided field of consciousness rather than physical sky alone. This move from bāhyākāśa to cidākāśa/non-spatial awareness is a recurrent Śaiva contemplative pattern.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Release Wherever the Mind Goes
sanskrit:
यि यि मनो यावत तत्तत् तेनैि तत्क्षणम् ।
ऩवरत्यज्यानिवस्थत्या वनस्तरङ्गस्ततो भिेत् ॥ १२९ ॥
translation: Wherever the mind goes, at each and every place, in that very moment, abandoning it there through non-fixation, one becomes thereafter waveless.
intent_summary: Do not chase or suppress the mind; wherever it moves, release fixation immediately and rest in stillness.
beginner_explanation: The mind keeps moving from one thing to another. This verse does not ask you to stop that by force. Instead, each time the mind lands somewhere, simply do not cling to it; then the mind gradually becomes calm, like water without ripples.
scholar_explanation: This is a subtle practice of anavasthitā or non-abidance: the yogin neither follows nor resists the mind's movement, but relinquishes fixation at the very point of contact. The result, nistaranga—wavelessness—signals a mind no longer generating secondary agitation around appearances. It exemplifies effortless awareness rather than concentrative exclusion.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Continuous Utterance of Bhairava
sanskrit:
भया सिधम् रियवत सिधदो व्याऩकोऽवखऱे ।
इवत भैरिशब्दस्य सन्ततोच्चारणावच्छि् ॥ १३० ॥
translation: Bhairava is the one who protects all, who is ever all-pervading throughout the whole. Thus, through the continuous utterance of the word 'Bhairava,' one becomes Śiva.
intent_summary: Contemplate and repeat the name Bhairava as the all-pervading protector until identity with Śiva awakens.
beginner_explanation: A sacred name can change the state of the mind when repeated with feeling and understanding. This verse recommends repeating 'Bhairava' while remembering that it points to the reality present everywhere. Over time, the repetition is meant to dissolve the sense of separation between you and that reality.
scholar_explanation: This verse treats the very word 'Bhairava' as mantra and contemplative revelation, grounded in an etymologizing description of Bhairava as universally protective and all-pervasive. Santatocchāraṇa, continuous utterance, is not merely vocal repetition but sustained mantric awareness in which nāma and tattva converge. The culmination in becoming Śiva reflects the nondual mantric principle that the deity-name, rightly realized, discloses one's own essential identity.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Beyond I-and-Mine into the Unsupported Mind
sanskrit:
अहं ममेदवमत्यावद प्रवतऩवत्तप्रसङ्गत् ।
वनराधारे मनो यावत तद्ध्यानप्रेरणाच्छमी ॥ १३१ ॥
translation: When the notions 'I' and 'mine' come to an end, and the stream of mental involvement subsides, as long as the mind rests without support (nirādhāra), through the impulse of that meditation one becomes pacified.
intent_summary: Let the possessive and egoic movements of mind fall away, allowing awareness to rest unsupported until profound peace dawns.
beginner_explanation: Usually the mind is busy saying 'I,' 'me,' and 'my problem.' This verse says that if those habits quiet down, the mind can rest without clinging to anything. In that unsupported resting, a deep calm appears on its own.
scholar_explanation: The OCR-distorted verse clearly points to the exhaustion of ahaṃ-mama-bhāva, the contracted structure of individuality and appropriation. Nirādhāra-manas here suggests consciousness no longer taking an object, support, or conceptual prop, a recurrent Trika theme in which cessation of vikalpa opens into Bhairava-awareness. The phrase taddhyāna-preraṇāc chamī/shamī indicates pacification (śama) through sustained contemplative orientation rather than suppression.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Meditation on the All-Pervading Support
sanskrit:
वनत्यो विभुवनधराधारो व्याऩकश्चावखऱावधऩ् ।
शब्दान्प्रवतऺणं ध्यायन्कृताथोऽथाधनुरूऩत् ॥ १३२ ॥
translation: The Eternal One is the support of the worlds, all-pervading and the sovereign of all. Meditating at every moment on these words, one becomes fulfilled, taking on that very form.
intent_summary: Contemplate continuously that reality is the all-pervading ground of everything, until your identity shifts into that universal presence.
beginner_explanation: This verse invites you to remember again and again that the deepest reality is everywhere and holds everything together. If you keep reflecting in this way, you stop feeling like a small separate self. Gradually, you begin to feel shaped by that vastness.
scholar_explanation: This is a śabda-based contemplative recognition of vibhutva, dhāratva/ādhāratva, and vyāpakatva—classical descriptors of Bhairava as the substrative and pervasive reality. Though framed through 'words' (śabdān), the practice is not mere repetition but nididhyāsana on the semantic force of these predicates until sādhaka and contemplated principle become of one form (tadrūpatā). It bridges conceptual contemplation and nondual assimilation.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Seeing the World as a Magical Non-Substance
sanskrit:
अतत्त्ववमन्द्रजाऱाभवमदं सिधमिवस्थतम् ।
वकं तत्त्ववमन्द्रजाऱस्य इवत दार्ढ्ाधच्छमं व्रजेत् ॥ १३३ ॥
translation: This whole manifested condition stands as non-tattva, like an illusion, like Indra's net of magic. Firmly inquiring, 'What is the reality of this magical display of non-tattva?' one enters peace.
intent_summary: Examine the apparent world as an illusory display lacking independent substance, and through that inquiry enter quiescent absorption.
beginner_explanation: Things seem solid and convincing, but this verse asks you to question that appearance. Look closely: is the world exactly as fixed and substantial as it seems? That deep questioning can loosen mental grip and bring quiet clarity.
scholar_explanation: The key gesture is vicāra into the ontological status of appearance: the phenomenal world is compared to indrajāla, the magician's display, familiar in Śaiva and Buddhist discourse alike. 'Atattva' does not mean absolute nonexistence but lack of self-standing reality apart from consciousness; inquiry into its status dislodges reified perception and leads to śama. This aligns with pratyabhijñā critiques of objectivity as a contracted presentation of Cit.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Knowledge and Action in the Self-Luminous Ground
sanskrit:
आत्मनो वनविधकारस्य क्व ऻानं क्व च िा वक्रया ।
ऻानायत्ता िवहभाधिा अत् शून्यवमदं जगत् ॥ १३४ ॥
translation: For the Self, whose nature is manifoldly manifesting light, where is knowledge, and where indeed is action? Since external manifestation depends upon knowledge, this world is empty (śūnya) [of separate reality].
intent_summary: Recognize that in the Self prior to division, knowledge and action are not truly separate, and that the world has no independent status apart from awareness.
beginner_explanation: We usually think there is a knower here, an action happening there, and a world outside. This verse says that before those divisions, there is one underlying awareness. Seen from that level, the world is empty of separateness.
scholar_explanation: The verse gestures toward the non-difference of jñāna and kriyā in the ātman, central to Kashmir Śaiva theology where icchā-jñāna-kriyā are powers of one Cit rather than separate functions. The statement that outward manifestation is dependent on knowing undermines naive realism; śūnyatā here is not nihilism but the absence of autonomous externality. The Self as prakāśa remains the illuminative ground in which epistemic and active distinctions arise secondarily.

speaker: Bhairava
title: No Bondage, No Liberation
sanskrit:
न मे िन्धो न मोऺो मे भीतस्यैता विभीवषका् ।
प्रवतविम्बवमदम् िुद्धेजधऱेवष्वि वििस्वत् ॥ १३५ ॥
translation: For me there is no bondage and no liberation; these are terrors only for the frightened. This is a reflection appearing in the intellects, like the reflection of the sun in water.
intent_summary: See bondage and liberation as conceptual appearances arising in mind, not as ultimate realities of the Self.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that from the deepest viewpoint, you are not truly trapped and do not need to become something else to be free. Bondage and liberation are ideas that matter only as long as fear and confusion remain. Like the sun reflected in water, they appear in the mind but do not change what you really are.
scholar_explanation: A radical advaitic declaration: bandha and mokṣa belong to the level of buddhi-pratibimba, not to the essential nature of Bhairava. The simile of the sun reflected in water preserves phenomenality while denying ultimate alteration in consciousness itself. This resonates strongly with Pratyabhijñā nondualism, where liberation is recognition (pratyabhijñā), not production of a new state.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Withdrawing from the Sense-Gates
sanskrit:
इवन्द्रयद्वारकं सिं सुखदु्खावदसम्गमम् ।
इतीवन्द्रयावण सम्त्यज्य स्वस्थ् स्वात्मवन ितधते ॥ १३६ ॥
translation: All contact with pleasure, pain, and the like comes through the doorway of the senses. Therefore, abandoning the senses, one becomes established in one's own Self-nature.
intent_summary: Notice that sensory contact generates the swing of pleasant and unpleasant experience, then turn inward and abide in the Self.
beginner_explanation: Pleasure and pain usually enter through seeing, hearing, touching, and the other senses. This verse suggests stepping back from being pulled around by those inputs. When attention is no longer scattered outward, it settles into a more steady inner presence.
